title: Writing practice: Kites, Beans and Water Bottles
description: Eight short writing tasks: retell a story, explain a math plan, use plant data, explain why a town grew, write a note, choose a book, explain a food chain, and ask for a water station.

stimuli.title: Story: Samir’s Blue Kite
paragraphs: Samir had a new blue kite. On Saturday he took it to the field with his sister Dalia. The wind was strong, so the kite jumped into the sky.

Then the string slipped out of Samir’s hand! The kite flew over the fence and landed in a tree. Samir felt sad. Dalia ran to find the caretaker, Mr. Ortiz. He brought a long pole and gently lifted the kite down. Samir smiled and said, “Thank you!” After that, he held the string with both hands.

stimuli.title: Math problem: Pencil packs
paragraphs: Ms. Rivera buys 7 packs of pencils. Each pack has 6 pencils. Her class has 28 students, and she wants to give each student 1 pencil.
She asks, “Do I have enough pencils?”

stimuli.title: Data table: Two bean plants
stimuli.caption: Two bean plants of the same kind grew for 14 days. They had the same soil and the same amount of water.

stimuli.title: Text: How Alderport Began
paragraphs: Long ago, farmers settled beside the Alder River. The river gave them fresh water for drinking and for crops. Its flat banks had rich soil.

Boats carried grain and wood to other towns, so the farmers could trade. Soon a market opened near the water. Families came to buy and sell, and more houses were built. Over time, the small settlement became the town of Alderport. Today, many people still live and work along the river.

stimuli.title: Scenario: Garden Day
paragraphs: Your friend Tomas was absent yesterday. Your class had Garden Day. This was the plan on the board:
Morning: plant bean seeds in paper cups. Late morning: water the cups and draw them. Before lunch: wash hands and put the tools away.
Tomas wants to know what happened.

stimuli.title: Two classmates talk about read-aloud books
paragraphs: Your class can choose one book to read aloud this month. Two classmates share ideas.
Dev says: “The Mapmaker’s Cat has 12 short chapters, so we can finish it in about two weeks. The cat solves puzzles with old maps. Many pages have drawings.”
Lina says: “Robot Garden has 20 chapters, so it would take about four weeks. A robot grows food for a town. It has few drawings, but the words are exciting.”

stimuli.title: Text: A Pond Food Chain
paragraphs: A small pond has a food chain with four living things. Pond plants use light from the Sun to make their own food. Snails eat the pond plants. Frogs eat the snails. Herons, which are tall birds, eat the frogs.

Each living thing gets the energy it needs from the food it eats. Scientists draw arrows in a food chain to show the way energy moves: from the plants to the snails, from the snails to the frogs, and from the frogs to the herons.

stimuli.title: Survey: Water at school
stimuli.caption: Results of a survey of 60 students at Hillside School.
rows: Do you bring a water bottle to school?
Is the line at the drinking fountain long at lunch?
Would you use a bottle-filling station?

items.stem: Retell the story “Samir’s Blue Kite” for a classmate who was absent. Tell what happened at the beginning, in the middle, and at the end.

checklist: I told who the story is about.
I told what happened first, next, and last.
I used time words such as first, then, and after that.
I told how Samir felt at the end.
exemplar: Task completion: retells the main events in order (the kite flies, the string slips, the kite lands in the tree, the caretaker helps).
Organization: has a clear beginning, middle, and end with time words.
Development: names the characters and includes at least one feeling.
Language: uses past-tense verbs consistently; pronouns (he, she, it) clearly refer back to characters.

support.clue: Find the problem in the story and who solves it. Notice the time words and what Samir does at the end.
support.frame: In the beginning, ______ had ______. Then ______. After that, ______. At the end, ______ felt ______ because ______.
support.model:
Mentor example about a different story. “In the beginning, Lena planted a seed. Then it rained for three days. After that, a small green leaf came up. At the end, Lena felt proud because she had helped it grow.” Notice how each sentence starts with a time word and uses past tense.

Retell your story in the same way.

items.stem: Explain how Ms. Rivera can find out whether she has enough pencils. Show each step with words and numbers, and tell what the answer means.

checklist: I told which numbers I used from the problem.
I told what operation I used and why.
I compared the total number of pencils to the number of students.
I used words such as because, so, and altogether.
exemplar: Task completion: identifies the operation (multiply 7 × 6) and states the total of 42 pencils.
Reasoning: compares 42 with 28 and concludes there are enough, with 14 left over.
Organization: steps are in a logical order with sequence words.
Vocabulary: uses mathematical terms such as multiply, total, compare, and left over.
Clarity: the final sentence tells what the answer means for the class.

support.clue: Find the two numbers that tell how many pencils there are in all. Then find the number you need to compare to.
support.frame: First, I found how many pencils there are in all by ______. That gives ______ pencils. Next, I ______. Because ______, ______.
support.model:
Mentor example about a different problem. “One shelf has 18 books and another shelf has 15 books. A class needs 30 books. First, I added 18 and 15 to find 33 books in all. Next, I compared 33 to 30. Because 33 is greater than 30, there are enough books, and 3 are left over.” Notice that each step has a reason.

Explain your problem in the same way.

items.stem: Do bean plants need light to grow well? Write a claim and support it with two pieces of evidence from the table.

checklist: I wrote a claim that answers the question.
I used numbers or colors from the table as evidence.
I used because or so to connect my claim and my evidence.
I told what was the same and what was different for the two plants.
exemplar: Task completion: states a clear claim (plants need light) and gives two pieces of evidence (6 leaves and green versus 2 leaves and pale yellow).
Reasoning: notes that soil and water were the same, so light is the difference.
Language: uses a connector such as because or so to link evidence to the claim.
Vocabulary: uses terms such as plant, light, leaves, and evidence.

support.clue: Compare the two rows. Look at what is different between Plant A and Plant B, and at what is the same.
support.frame: I claim that plants ______ light to ______. The table shows that Plant A had ______ and Plant B had ______. This evidence shows that ______.
support.model:
Mentor example about a different topic. “I claim that seeds need water to sprout. The table shows that Cup 1, with water, had 5 sprouts and Cup 2, with no water, had 0 sprouts. This evidence shows that water helps seeds begin to grow.” Notice that the claim comes first and the numbers come next.

Write your claim and evidence in the same way.

facts: Plants use light to make their food, so a plant kept without light grows poorly.
In the table, only the amount of light was different between Plant A and Plant B.

items.stem: Explain why the town of Alderport grew beside the river. Give at least two reasons from the text and tell how each reason helped people.

checklist: I gave at least two reasons.
I told how each reason helped people.
I used words such as because, so, and as a result.
I used details from the text.
exemplar: Task completion: gives two or more reasons from the text (water, rich soil, trade by boat, a market).
Development: explains the effect of each reason on people’s lives.
Cohesion: connectors such as because, so, and as a result link reasons to effects.
Vocabulary: uses terms such as settle, trade, market, and crops.
Organization: reasons are presented one at a time.

support.clue: Find the sentences that tell what the river gave the farmers. Notice what happened after the boats came.
support.frame: The town of Alderport grew near the river for two main reasons. One reason is that ______. This helped people because ______. Another reason is that ______. As a result, ______.
support.model:
Mentor example about a different place. “A fishing village grew beside a bay for two reasons. One reason is that the bay had many fish. This helped families because they could catch food every day. Another reason is that the bay was calm. As a result, small boats could leave and return safely.” Notice that each reason is followed by how it helped.

Explain your town in the same way.

facts: Rivers can provide fresh water, rich soil, and a way to move goods by boat.
Alderport is an invented town used only for this practice.

items.stem: Write a short note to Tomas. Tell him what your class did on Garden Day and what you liked best.

checklist: I started with Dear Tomas and ended with my name.
I told what we did first, next, and last.
I told one thing I liked and why.
I used past-tense words such as planted and watered.
exemplar: Task completion: tells the three parts of the day in order and names a favorite part.
Format: uses a greeting and a closing that suit a note to a friend.
Language: uses past-tense verbs and time words such as first, then, and later.
Development: gives a reason for the favorite part.

support.clue: Use the plan on the board. Notice the three parts of the day and write them in order.
support.frame: Dear Tomas, yesterday we had Garden Day. First, we ______. Then we ______. Before lunch, we ______. My favorite part was ______ because ______. Your friend, ______
support.model:
Mentor example about a different event. “Dear Ana, on Friday we had a book fair. First, we walked to the library. Then we looked at the books. After that, we each chose one book. My favorite part was the picture books because they were funny. Your friend, Ben.” Notice the greeting, the time words, and the closing.

Write your note to Tomas in the same way.

items.stem: Which book should the class read aloud this month? Write a paragraph to convince your teacher. Use at least two details from Dev and Lina.

checklist: I wrote which book I choose.
I gave at least two reasons with details from the text.
I told one reason someone might choose the other book.
I ended with a sentence that repeats my choice.
exemplar: Task completion: states a clear choice and supports it with two or more details (chapters, time, drawings, story idea).
Reasoning: connects each detail to why it matters for reading aloud this month.
Organization: opens with a claim and closes with a conclusion.
Cohesion: uses connectors such as first, also, however, and for these reasons.
Audience: the tone suits a paragraph written to a teacher.

support.clue: Underline the numbers and details in each comment. Decide which details matter most for reading aloud this month.
support.frame: I think our class should read ______ because ______. First, ______. Also, ______. Some students may prefer ______, but ______. For these reasons, ______.
support.model:
Mentor example about a different choice. “I think our class should choose the park for the picnic because it is close. First, we can walk there in ten minutes. Also, it has shade under big trees. Some students may prefer the beach, but it is too far to walk. For these reasons, the park is the better choice.” Notice how the writer answers the other side.

Write your own paragraph in the same way.

facts: Dev says The Mapmaker’s Cat has 12 chapters and takes about two weeks.
Lina says Robot Garden has 20 chapters and takes about four weeks.

items.stem: Explain how energy from the Sun reaches the heron in this pond. Then predict what would happen to the snails, the frogs, and the herons if the pond plants died. Use details from the text.

checklist: I explained each link in the food chain in order.
I told where the energy starts.
I explained what would happen if the plants died and why.
I used science words such as energy, food chain, and plants.
I connected my ideas with words like because and as a result.
exemplar: Task completion: traces energy from the Sun to the plants, snails, frogs, and heron, and makes a prediction about the plants dying.
Reasoning: the prediction follows the chain (less food for snails, then frogs, then herons).
Organization: events are in order, with the prediction in a separate part.
Vocabulary and structures: uses academic words and complex sentences with because, so, and if.
Cohesion: ties each living thing to the one before it.

support.clue: Follow the arrows in the second paragraph one link at a time. Then ask yourself: who needs the plants first, and who needs the next animal?
support.frame: Energy starts with the ______. The plants ______. The snails get energy when they ______. Then the frogs ______, and the herons ______. If the plants died, the snails would ______ because ______. As a result, ______.
support.model:
Mentor example about a different chain of events. “In a school, the bakery makes bread for the cafeteria. If the bakery closed, the cafeteria would have no bread, so it could make fewer sandwiches. As a result, fewer students could buy lunch.” Notice how each effect leads to the next one.

Explain the pond food chain in the same way.

facts: Plants use light from the Sun to make food.
Animals get energy by eating plants or other animals.
If the plants at the start of a food chain die, the animals that depend on them have less food.

items.stem: Write a letter to Principal Okafor. Ask her to put a bottle-filling station near the cafeteria. Give at least two reasons and use numbers from the survey.

checklist: I used a greeting and a closing.
I told clearly what I am asking for.
I gave at least two reasons with numbers from the survey.
I used a polite voice for a principal.
I ended by thanking her.
exemplar: Task completion: states a clear request and supports it with two or more survey numbers.
Format and audience: uses a greeting, a closing, and polite, respectful phrasing.
Reasoning: explains why each number matters (for example, 45 of 60 already bring bottles).
Organization: request, reasons, and closing are in separate parts.
Language: uses polite request phrases and connectors such as first, also, and for these reasons.

support.clue: Find the rows that tell how many students already have bottles, how many wait in line, and how many would use a station. Decide which numbers best support your request.
support.frame: Dear Principal Okafor, I am writing to ask you to ______. First, the survey shows that ______ out of 60 students ______. Second, ______. For these reasons, ______. Thank you for ______. Sincerely, ______
support.model:
Mentor example about a different request. “Dear Mr. Haddad, I am writing to ask for a longer recess on Fridays. First, in our survey, 40 of 50 students said they would like more time to play. Second, 35 students said they are tired after long lessons. For these reasons, a longer recess would help us. Thank you for thinking about my request. Sincerely, Priya.” Notice the polite words and the numbers.

Write your letter in the same way.

facts: The survey numbers in the table are invented for this practice.
